candidates.title: fix(mkv-core): extract mode lets .mkv/.MKV siblings overwrite each other's sidecars
candidates.taskDescription:
Follow-up to #175, which refuses colliding destinations in remux mode only.

## Problem

Extract mode has the same collision. Discovery reads the `.mkv` extension case-insensitively (`scan.rs`), so `Show - 01.mkv` and `Show - 01.MKV` in one directory are two items with the same file stem. `extract.rs` names every sidecar from that stem:

- subtitle: `{stem}_{EpLabel}{ep}_{lang}_track{id}.ass`
- chapters: `{stem}_{EpLabel}{ep}_chapters.xml`
- cover: `{stem}_cover{ext}`

The subtitle and chapter files are promoted with `promote_file`, which replaces an existing file, so the second item silently overwrites the first one's sidecars, and both report success. The cover is skipped when `{stem}_cover{ext}` already exists, so the second item keeps the first one's cover. Under `--out-dir` the same happens for mirrored directories that differ only by case (`Season 1/` and `season 1/`).

Not reproduced with real media yet; this is from reading `extract.rs` next to the remux repro.

## Suggested direction

Mirror #175's remux check: after selected-items filtering and before any media work, refuse an extract batch whose items share a sidecar stem in the same destination directory, compared case-folded, naming the colliding Item IDs. The track ids and episode labels are only known after probing, so comparing `(destination dir, file stem)` is the simple, conservative key. #175 added `pipeline::validate_remux_destinations`; reuse or generalize it rather than adding a second rule.

## Tests

- A plan-only test with `.mkv`/`.MKV` siblings in extract mode.
- A `test_real_remux`-style extract case if the existing suite has one to extend.

candidates.title: istep not passed to `compute_loss` during validation (context-loss warmup stuck at 0)
candidates.taskDescription:
# Description

Follow-up to #2720 / #2722 (on `develop-ssl-diffusion-v1`). The training path now passes `istep`
through `LossCalculator.compute_loss` to the loss modules, but the validation call does not:

`src/weathergen/train/trainer.py` (validate):
```python
_ = self.loss_calculator_val.compute_loss(
    preds=preds,
    targets_and_aux=targets_and_auxs,
    metadata=extract_batch_metadata(batch),
)
```

So `istep` defaults to 0 in `LossLatentSSLStudentTeacher.compute_loss`. With
`context_loss.warmup_steps > 0`, the warmup factor is always 0 during validation:

- the context loss never contributes to the total validation loss, so validation and training
  losses can't be compared
- `context_warmup` is logged as 0 for validation

Training gradients are not affected. As with #2720, this is silent.

# Fix

Pass `istep=self.cf.general.istep` in the validation `compute_loss` call.

candidates.title: Extract batch runner / Ralph loop / circuit breaker out of core - should be a tool built on the runner
candidates.taskDescription:
## Context

Follow-up to discussion in #8. Comparing our core against LangChain/LangGraph turned up real overlap - see the wheel-reimplementation analysis below.

## Overlap findings

| Our code | LangGraph/LangChain equivalent | Overlap |
|---|---|---|
| `WorkflowEngine` + `PhaseExecutor` + `routing.ts` | LangGraph `StateGraph` (nodes, edges, conditional routing) | High |
| `ContextStore` (disk persistence, resume) | LangGraph checkpointers (SQLite/Postgres/memory) with built-in resume/replay | High |
| Gate system `user_approval` pauses | LangGraph `interrupt()` / human-in-the-loop breakpoints | High |
| `AgentRunner` provider abstraction (`OpenAiRunner`, `AnthropicRunner`) | LangChain `ChatModel` interface | Medium-high |

## Proposal

1. **Batch runner should be dropped from core and extracted as a separate tool built on top of the runner**, not embedded in `src/batch.ts` as part of the engine package. Specifically:
   - **Batch execution** (multi-ticket sequential runs)
   - **Ralph loop** (`--max-iterations`, re-running a ticket N times)
   - **Circuit breaker** (stop after N consecutive failures)

   None of these are workflow-engine concerns - they're orchestration/ops concerns that should sit *on top of* a stable `workflow_run` API (CLI or MCP), the same way a cron job or CI pipeline would drive it. Keeping them in core couples engine changes to batch-runner changes and duplicates what a thin wrapper script/tool could do.

2. Open question (not part of this issue, tracked separately): whether `WorkflowEngine`/`ContextStore`/gate-pause machinery should eventually be rebuilt on LangGraph instead of hand-rolled, given the high overlap with `StateGraph` + checkpointer + `interrupt()`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `src/batch.ts` (batch runner, Ralph loop, circuit breaker) removed from the core package
- [ ] Same functionality re-implemented as a standalone tool/script that calls the runner's public API (CLI invocation or MCP `workflow_run`) instead of importing engine internals
- [ ] Docs updated to reflect batch/Ralph/circuit-breaker as an external tool, not a core feature
- [ ] Core package README no longer advertises batch runner as a first-class surface

## Non-goals
- This issue does not cover replacing WorkflowEngine/ContextStore with LangGraph - that's a separate, bigger decision to be discussed first.

candidates.title: Dedupe map assets and bake static batches at extract time
candidates.taskDescription:
## Problem
`sekiro-extract map` writes each block's own copy of shared models and DDS textures, so connected blocks load byte-identical assets under different paths.
PR #117 (#98) undoes this at runtime: it hashes and compares every streamed texture and mesh, aliases render assets, and retires static-batch source meshes from the GPU by editing Bevy's extraction queue.
That works (9.5 GB to 7.4 GB on m11_00) but costs CPU while blocks stream in and depends on Bevy internals.

## To do
- Extract shared textures and models once to a shared, content-addressed folder (or remap paths in the loader), so the asset server dedupes by path and `texture_residency.rs` and `share_sources` in `mesh_residency.rs` can go.
- Bake static batches at extract time, so their source meshes never load to the GPU and the residency surgery in `mesh_residency.rs` can go.
- Skip top mips in a DDS loader setting instead of slicing loaded images in `vram.rs`.

## Done when
- m11_00 peak VRAM is the same or lower than with #117, the three runtime dedupe paths are removed, and the first 20 s of play stutter less.

candidates.title: Improve image-export throughput with persistent workers, bounded parallelism, and pipelined archive batches
candidates.taskDescription:
## Problem

Large image selections spend substantial time preparing inputs before Slurm processing starts.

On our local Windows/Docker Desktop deployment, a sample of 40 images averaged approximately:

| Stage | Average per image |
|---|---:|
| Zarr export | 4.1 seconds |
| Pixel-identity checks and canonical promotion attempt | 1.0 second |
| Total preparation | 5.1 seconds |

Each image contained approximately 16 MB of raw pixels. This corresponds to approximately 3.2 MB/s of **raw pixel-equivalent preparation throughput**, not network-transfer throughput.

The inspected implementation exports images sequentially, launches an `omero zarr` subprocess for each fresh export, and waits for export and packaging to finish before transferring and unpacking the archive.

These local measurements motivate the proposal, but should not be treated as production performance estimates.

Relevant code: [`_data/_SLURM_Image_Transfer.py`](https://github.com/NL-BioImaging/biomero-scripts/blob/master/_data/_SLURM_Image_Transfer.py).

## Target environments

The design should support both:

- **Local development:** Windows/Docker Desktop, limited resources, and Windows-mounted working directories.
- **Production:** Red Hat Linux, 48 CPUs, 512 GB RAM, and fast local storage. Original files reside on a mounted NAS with a maximum connection speed of **10 Gbit/s**.

The NAS connection has a theoretical ceiling of approximately **1.25 GB/s before overhead**. Additional workers should improve concurrency until CPU, OMERO, storage, or NAS throughput becomes the limiting factor. Worker count should therefore be configurable and measured, rather than automatically set to all 48 CPUs.

## Suggested design

### 1. Reuse exporter processes and connections

Introduce a pool of long-lived export workers.

Each worker would:

- Initialize its exporter and OMERO connection once.
- Export multiple images through that connection.
- Maintain session keepalive and reconnect after recoverable failures.
- Close its resources on completion or cancellation.

Investigate using a supported Python exporter API or a persistent adapter around `omero-cli-zarr`, avoiding repeated interpreter initialization and connection setup.

Each worker should own its connection and mutable reader state. Process workers should initialize connections after starting, rather than inherit live connections through a fork.

### 2. Add bounded parallel exports

Allow several independent images to export concurrently.

Preassign deterministic output paths and manifest entries using image IDs and HCS field paths. Completion order must not affect naming, image ordering, or provenance.

For plate exports, workers should write separate field subtrees or temporary stores. A coordinator should finalize shared plate/well metadata, avoiding concurrent writes to shared metadata files.

Concurrency should respect:

- Actual CPU and memory allocations.
- Per-worker codec thread counts.
- Estimated decoded-image memory.
- Available scratch space.
- Observed NAS and OMERO throughput.

Large images should continue using bounded tile/chunk processing.

### 3. Overlap export, archive creation, transfer, and extraction

The current implementation already creates ZIP archives. The proposed improvement is to create **multiple independent archive batches** and overlap the stages:

```text
Export batch N+1
    while packaging/transferring batch N
        while extracting batch N-1
```

A bounded queue between stages would prevent exports from filling scratch storage when transfer or extraction falls behind.

Batch boundaries could use a combination of:

- Maximum bytes.
- Maximum number of images or fields.
- Maximum waiting time before closing a partially filled batch.

For example, benchmark batches around **1-4 GiB**, with an image-count limit and a time-based flush. These should be tuning options, not fixed assumptions.

Each archive should have one writer. Parallel packaging and extraction should operate on separate archives.

For Zarr, retain stored/uncompressed ZIP as an option: chunk data may already be compressed, making additional compression expensive with little benefit. Benchmark compression choices against actual transfer bandwidth.

### 4. Extract batches independently and publish inputs atomically

Transfer completed archives while later batches are still being produced. Extract several archives concurrently into separate staging directories on fast destination storage.

A coordinator should assemble the final input layout and publish an "inputs ready" marker only when all required batches are complete.

Archive batching should preserve the existing analysis boundary: a workflow expecting a complete plate should still receive that complete plate before submission.

For a local deployment where both stages can access the same storage, consider a direct local-copy/staging transport that avoids unnecessary archive-and-extract work.

### 5. Make the pipeline resumable and capacity-aware

Maintain a manifest containing image/field mappings, batch membership, sizes, completion status, and integrity information.

The pipeline should support:

- Retrying a failed image or archive without repeating successful work.
- Transferring archives under temporary names and publishing them atomically.
- Cancelling active exporters, transfers, and extraction workers.
- Limiting queued batches and total staging bytes.
- Cleaning temporary data according to the existing retention policy.
- Preserving source files and valid canonical stores.

Existing pixel-identity checks should remain intact. The identity mismatches observed locally need separate investigation; this optimization must not bypass them.

## Suggested initial benchmark settings

These are starting points for testing, not promised optimal values:

| Stage | Local deployment | Production starting point |
|---|---:|---:|
| Export workers | 2 | 8; compare 4, 8, 16, and 24 |
| Archive writers | 1 | 1-2 |
| Transfer workers | 1 | 1-2, depending on the destination link |
| Extraction workers | 1 | 2-4 |

Measure the NAS source link and the processor-to-Slurm transfer link separately. Increasing transfer concurrency cannot remove a bottleneck in the initial NAS reads.

## Benchmark and acceptance criteria

Compare the existing implementation against connection reuse, parallel export, archive pipelining, and their combination.

Record:

- End-to-end time until inputs are ready.
- Export, identity-check, packaging, transfer, and extraction times.
- Images/s, raw pixel-equivalent MB/s, archive MB/s, and NAS read throughput.
- CPU utilization, peak memory, scratch-space usage, and queue lengths.
- Cold-cache and warm-cache performance.
- Cancellation, retry, and interrupted-transfer behavior.

The new path should preserve pixel values, channels, axes, physical calibration, HCS structure, labels, and provenance. It should retain a single-worker compatibility mode and produce clear progress for each preparation stage.

## Repository coordination

The main coordination belongs in `biomero-scripts`. Reusable transfer, resumability, and remote extraction functionality may require corresponding changes in [`biomero`](https://github.com/NL-BioImaging/biomero/blob/main/biomero/slurm_client.py). Deployment settings and documentation would belong in [`NL-BIOMERO`](https://github.com/NL-BioImaging/NL-BIOMERO).

candidates.title: bloomctl: batch-ingest-result doesn't cross-check RunManifest.pipeline_run_id against envelope provenance
candidates.taskDescription:
## Context

Found during review of bloom #678 / PR #697 (scope `cyl batch-ingest-result` discovery to the RunManifest).

## The gap

`discover_envelopes` scopes discovery purely by **scan_key** (matching a manifest's `scan_keys` against filename stems). `RunManifest.pipeline_run_id` is a required field, successfully parsed, but never read or compared against anything - in particular, never cross-checked against the ingested envelope's own `provenance.pipeline_run_id` (an independent field, already forwarded verbatim to the write-back RPC).

This means: if `envelopes_dir` is reused across two different pipeline runs, and a stale file from a **prior** run happens to declare the same `scan_key` the **current** run's manifest also declares, the stale file passes the scope check unmodified - scan_key identity is checked, but run identity isn't. This is the sharpest remaining form of the original "stale file gets silently ingested" contamination bloom #678 was meant to close, just narrowed to the specific case of a scan_key collision across runs (rather than an unrelated scan_key lingering from a prior run, which #678 does catch).

## Not a regression - matches upstream's own scope

Neither `sleap-roots-predict`'s `discover_scans` (predict #35) nor `sleap-roots`'s `extract_batch` (sleap-roots #263) - the two reference implementations bloom #678 mirrors - cross-check `pipeline_run_id` either. This is a pre-existing, accepted limitation across the whole chain, not something #678 introduced or was expected to close on its own.

## Suggested fix direction

Since `provenance.pipeline_run_id` is already present on ingested envelopes and forwarded unmodified to the RPC, `ingest_one_envelope` (or a caller) could compare it against the manifest's `pipeline_run_id` that scoped the file's discovery, rejecting or flagging a mismatch. This is a bigger, separate change than pure discovery scoping - validating envelope provenance against manifest identity is a different mechanism than filename/scan_key matching - and would need its own OpenSpec proposal given the size (and ideally should land consistently across all three repos in the chain: predict, traits, and write-back, not just write-back alone).

## References

- PR #697: https://github.com/Salk-Harnessing-Plants-Initiative/bloom/pull/697
- bloom #678
- sleap-roots-pipeline #37 (cross-repo manifest-scoping tracker)
- `openspec/changes/add-cyl-writeback-manifest-scope/design.md`

candidates.title: Safe archive entry names for batch uploads
candidates.taskDescription:
## Story

As a caller who extracts the batch archive, I want every entry name to be safe on common file systems, so that extracting the ZIP never fails or produces a misleading file.

## Background

Batch entry names come from the validated `FileName` (ADR-0011, "Names"), which already rejects path separators, `.` and `..`. Reviewing the batch session (#114, PR #130) showed names it still accepts that are unsafe or confusing once they become archive entries:

- drive-relative and alternate-data-stream forms: `C:evil.txt`, `a.txt:s.txt`
- reserved device names: `CON.txt`
- Unicode format characters such as the right-to-left override, which makes a name display differently from what it is
- names of any length: a 70,004-character name is accepted, while file systems and extractors stop at 255 bytes (multipart headers cap real requests near 16 KB)
- names that differ only in Unicode normalization (`é.txt` composed vs decomposed) count as distinct for duplicate detection but are the same file on some file systems

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A Domain rule for archive entry names rejects names longer than 255 UTF-8 bytes
- [ ] rejects `:`, `<`, `>`, `"`, `|`, `?`, `*` and control characters
- [ ] rejects Windows reserved device names (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9), with or without an extension, case-insensitively
- [ ] rejects Unicode format characters (category Cf)
- [ ] batch duplicate detection compares names in normalization form C; the emitted entry name is unchanged
- [ ] a rejected name becomes an `InvalidFileName` row, like the existing rules
- [ ] each rule has a Domain test

## Out of scope

- Changing the single-file endpoint: v0.3 keeps its behaviour unchanged, so the rules apply to batch entry names only.
- Repairing or transliterating names: an unsafe name is rejected, not fixed.
- Changing how duplicates are numbered.

candidates.title: ANTIRRUIDO - auditar y depurar ramas históricas de Knowledge y PC con evidencia de conservación
candidates.taskDescription:
## Hallazgo / objetivo

Tras cerrar **MVP5 (#113)** y **fidelidad p0192 (#114)**, los repositorios CarpiNova-Knowledge y CarpiNova-PC tienen **cero Issues y PR abiertos** y sus CI de integración están GREEN. La revisión de antirruido detectó **377 ramas remotas en Knowledge** (376 fuera de `main`) y **56 en PC** (55 fuera de `main`) = **431 referencias no-main**. No confundir este conteo con commits o archivos duplicados.

**Objetivo:** clasificar esas referencias, demostrar qué ramas pueden retirarse sin perder trabajo, evidencia o capacidad de rollback, y **solo entonces** ejecutar una limpieza limitada, aprobada y reversible. Sin modificar código, contrato, contenido fuente ni CI. **Carpinova-Agente queda explícitamente fuera de alcance.**

### Identidad inicial verificada (2026-10-20)

- Knowledge main: `d350f3de1104977986f30498d212e018cbac5d29`; [postmerge QA #39503373699](https://github.com/sierraglobalcompany-rgb/CarpiNova-Knowledge/actions/runs/39503373699) SUCCESS, 451 pruebas.
- PC main: `f78a7316bad14641338e4a0fd567e759b0dfb8e5`; [Consumer Proof #39494993658](https://github.com/sierraglobalcompanyv2/CarpiNova-PC/actions/runs/39494993658) SUCCESS, 175 pruebas, hashes/artefactos verificados.
- Ambos: ningún Issue o PR abierto durante la inspección.

### Hallazgo PC ya comprobado

De 55 ramas distintas de `main`, la comparación contra el SHA real de PC da **52 ramas cuyo commit es ancestro de `main`** (`ahead=0`; `behind>0`), agrupadas en 12 HEAD/SHA distintos. Hay **3 ramas divergentes** (`ahead>0`): `audit/mvp3-knowledge-integration-20261013`, `codex/issue108-final-semantic-sheet` y `governance/four-laws-design-20261017`. **Las tres quedan en REVIEW/HOLD**; no asumir que un diff antiguo esté o no cubierto por squash sin análisis.

Las 52 ramas ancestrales son **candidatas**, no autorizaciones de borrado. Comprobar consumidores de nombres de rama, documentación, releases, workflows, dependencias externas y valor forense antes de clasificar DELETE.

### Hallazgo Knowledge

Hay ramas históricas de tipo `audit/`, `checkpoint/`, `extract/`, `feat/`, `feature/`, `test/`, `tmp/` y otras. Una muestra comparativa demuestra estados mixtos: algunas apuntan a commits ancestros de `main`; otras tienen commits únicos por divergencia o squash. Por ejemplo `extract/batch-025` presenta `ahead=22` y `behind=499`; **mantener REVIEW**, no borrado automático. La rama fusionada `fix/knowledge-p0192-hidrosanitary-site-survey` también es divergente por el squash: el árbol funcional está representado en `main`, pero sus SHAs no están en ancestry lineal. Los conteos Knowledge requieren inventario exhaustivo previo.

## Plan ejecutable mínimo (KISS)

1. **Snapshot read-only** de la lista completa de ramas de ambos repositorios, con SHA y protección. Registrar SHA de ambos `main`, Issues y PR abiertos y hora UTC.
2. **Clasificar cada referencia** con `git merge-base --is-ancestor` / GitHub Compare, diff/árbol, PR fusionado y referencias usadas por docs/workflows/releases; marcar `KEEP`, `DELETE_CANDIDATE`, `REVIEW` o `ACTIVE`. No equiparar `status=diverged` con pérdida de trabajo, pero no borrarla por deducción.
3. **Evidencia mínima por lote**: rama+SHA exacto, `ahead/behind`, confirmación de árbol/historial representado, PR/issue, referencias y ruta de recuperación. Guardar inventario como **artefacto de revisión fuera de los repositorios**, no commitear checkpoints duplicados.
4. **Gate de aprobación del propietario** con listado y conteo exactos. Sin aprobación **NO borrar ramas**. No crear workflows temporales o scripts persistentes.
5. Solo tras aprobación: borrar en lotes pequeños con verificación de SHA/head inmediatamente antes de cada borrado; nunca tocar `main` ni ramas activas/ambiguas. Revalidar lista y supervivencia de commits/trabajo.
6. Confirmar invariantes: SHAs de `main` intactos, PR/Issues intactos, CI sin degradación. Cerrar cuando no queden candidatos aprobados pendientes; los REVIEW quedan documentados sin forzar decisión.

## Reglas vinculantes

Las cuatro leyes de ambos `AGENTS.md`: **KISS, Antirruido, Antiparches, Diseño**. Precedencia de GitHub real y fuente canónica. Priorizar eliminar ruido únicamente con prueba de seguridad. Git history conserva historia normal, pero **no asumir** que todos los commits de ramas divergentes están integrados.

**NO-TOUCH:** `Carpinova-Agente`, datos canónicos, PDF, source manifests, Knowledge distribution, UI, contratos, feature work, deployment. No force push. No cambios de `main`. No cerrar con limpieza especulativa.

**Criterio de aceptación inmediato:** inventario completo y clasificación rigurosa de ramas, listado separado de `DELETE_CANDIDATE` y `REVIEW`, aprobación explícita solicitada antes de cualquier eliminación.

candidates.title: unstructured2graph: GLiNER2Backend has no cross-chunk coreference and no batched reconciliation path (LightRAG has both)
candidates.taskDescription:
## What

GLiNER2Backend (#330) and LightRAGBackend are both `ExtractionBackend` implementations, but two aspects of LightRAG's behavior have no GLiNER2 equivalent today. Neither is a bug (#336/#338 already fixed the actual bug, GLiNER2's context-window truncation) -- these are architecture gaps worth closing deliberately.

### 1. No cross-chunk entity coreference

LightRAG's LLM merges "the same" entity mentioned across different chunks/documents into one canonical node, with a merged description. `GLiNER2Backend._entity_id` is deliberately scoped to `(chunk_hash, entity_type, normalized_text)` -- documented in its own docstring as a known limitation: "unlike LightRAG, this backend does no cross-chunk coreference -- the same real-world entity mentioned in two different chunks becomes two separate Memgraph nodes."

This matters more than it used to: post-#331, a session is one document/chunk, so within a session this is less of an issue, but across sessions (the common case -- the same person, team, or project recurring over many sessions) GLiNER2 will keep creating duplicate nodes indefinitely, where LightRAG consolidates them.

Closing this is a real design decision, not a quick fix: what counts as "the same" entity (exact normalized text? embedding similarity? a threshold?), and where the merge/upsert step lives (write time, per session? a periodic post-process?).

### 2. No batched/parallel reconciliation path

LightRAG has `SessionsGraph.reconcile_sessions_batch()` (#333): many sessions staged into one shared LightRAG worker-pool pass, `context_graph_eval.reconcile_batch`'s default path. GLiNER2 only has the plain sequential `reconcile_session` loop (`_reconcile_batch_gliner2` in `context_graph_eval/reconcile.py`, added for the GLiNER2 eval-pipeline work) -- one session at a time, `await`ed in order.

Unlike LightRAG's concurrency (network-bound API calls, safe to run many at once), GLiNER2 model-instance concurrency is *not* clearly safe -- checked directly: `batch_extract`/`extract_long` call `self.eval()` and lazily cache `self._inference_collator` on every invocation, with no documented thread-safety guarantee, so firing multiple `asyncio.to_thread` calls at the same model instance from separate sessions is a real race risk (benign at best, a corrupted result at worst), not something to just try.

GLiNER2 does have a real equivalent already in the library, unused: `model.batch_extract(texts, schema, ...)` performs genuine vectorized batching -- one tokenization/forward pass over many texts together, safe because it's a single call, not concurrent calls. Measured (short synthetic texts, `fastino/gliner2.5-base-v1`): 20 texts sequentially via `extract()` took 3.05s, the same 20 via one `batch_extract()` call took 2.36s (1.29x) -- a real, if modest, win on short text; likely larger on the longer real session texts `extract_long`'s own windowing already produces many chunks for.

## Why it matters

Both gaps are specifically about **parity between the two backends as pluggable options**, not about either one being broken:

- Coreference gap: a real graph-quality difference a user switching from LightRAG to GLiNER2 would hit silently -- more duplicate nodes over time, no error.
- Batching gap: GLiNER2's own reconciliation path is currently slower than it needs to be for a multi-session batch (like the 100-question Tier 1 eval run), purely from the lack of batching, independent of #336's fix.

## Suggested fix

1. **Batching (lower-risk, do first)**: give `_reconcile_batch_gliner2` a batched variant using `model.batch_extract()` across multiple sessions' texts in one call, rather than looping `reconcile_session` one at a time. Needs `GLiNER2Backend` to expose a batch-shaped entry point (`aingest_chunks`, plural, alongside the existing `aingest_chunk`) so callers outside the eval pipeline benefit too, not just this one caller.
2. **Coreference (real design work, do second)**: needs its own discussion on identity/merge semantics before implementation -- not sized here.

<sub>Found while comparing GLiNER2Backend and LightRAGBackend after landing #338 (map: unstructured2graph pluggable backends, #330).</sub>

candidates.title: Extract: batch several exchanges per claude -p invocation
candidates.taskDescription:
## Measurement

Every LLM call spawns a fresh `claude -p` with `--no-session-persistence` in a new temp cwd (`infovore/llm/claude_cli.py:93`), so the CLI's own system prompt is re-sent on every call and prompt caching can never read back.

`extraction_runs` for `claude-sonnet-5`: 12,246 ok runs, avg **7,616 input tokens** per exchange.

Rendering the real prompt offline for 30 recent exchanges (`build_request` + `render_prompt`, no API call) gives our actual payload:

| part | tokens |
|---|---|
| user prompt (mean of 30) | ~1,820 |
| `SYSTEM_PROMPT` | ~471 |
| `ExtractionOut` JSON schema | ~252 |
| **our content** | **~2,543** |
| **billed** | **7,616** |
| **harness overhead** | **~5,073 (67%)** |

The overhead is per *spawn*, not per exchange.

## Proposal

Send N exchanges (default 10) per invocation, returning a JSON array of per-exchange results keyed by index. Amortises the ~5,073 tokens to ~507 per exchange, taking input from ~7,616 to ~3,050, a ~60% cut on the input side.

- Per-exchange failure handling unchanged; a malformed batch falls back to per-exchange calls for that batch.
- Each exchange keeps its own `extraction_runs` row. Token counts are only available per call, so record the batch's usage plus the batch size and divide, or add a `batch_tokens`/`batch_size` pair rather than silently attributing the whole batch to one row.
- Compare against per-exchange extraction on the same exchanges before switching: claim counts, and any claim the batched run drops.

Sibling of #126, which proposes the same for probe. Probe is the bigger win by call volume (~77,670 spawns vs ~12,656), so #126 should land first.

## Constraint

No Anthropic API access on this account (Max 2x), so the Batch API and explicit prompt caching are not options. Amortising spawns is the lever that is available.

candidates.title: Validate and reduce GPU synchronization and transfer overhead in ranker training
candidates.taskDescription:
<!-- performance-audit-followup: 2026-10-24/training-cuda-overhead -->
**Execution:** human-required  
**Audit item:** Performance follow-up 5/8 (24 October 2026)

## Problem / why this costs time
Training and validation extract a host loss scalar every batch. Calibration extracts five metric scalars per batch. On CUDA, these host reads introduce synchronization points. DataLoaders use default pageable memory and transfers use blocking `tensor.to(device)`. A CPU profiler around the actual evaluation functions with two fixture batches observed 3 scalar-extraction events for validation and 11 for calibration, including one DataLoader setup extraction in each run. No CUDA device was available; GPU stall duration and speedup are unknown.

## Requirements
- Human input required: provide an approved CUDA benchmark environment and review workload, resource/cost limits and the measured configuration before adopting GPU-specific defaults.
- Preserve loss definitions, example weighting, calibration semantics, split ordering, artifact provenance and CPU support.
- Accumulate detached metric tensors without retaining training graphs; define numerical tolerances explicitly.
- Do not automatically add DataLoader workers or enable mixed precision/converted artifacts under this scope.

## Proposed fix
Accumulate metric totals on device and transfer only at reporting boundaries. Compare CUDA-only pinned-memory/nonblocking transfers and representative batch sizes against the current path. Keep the simpler CPU path unless evidence supports a change.

## Acceptance / verification
- [ ] Record hardware/software identity, batch sizes, profiler synchronization traces, epoch time, examples/second and memory for baseline/treatment.
- [ ] Training/validation losses and per-head calibration agree within documented tolerances; no graph or memory retention regression occurs.
- [ ] CPU execution and small in-memory datasets retain acceptable performance; unavailable hardware results are reported honestly.
- [ ] An explicit benchmark decision records supported settings and rollback; no hardware provisioning or production model activation is implied.

## Dependencies / cross-repo context
No confirmed hard dependency. [ACM-VIT/Weave-ml#67](https://github.com/ACM-VIT/Weave-ml/issues/67) concerns inference-device and converted-artifact selection; this issue covers training transfers and metric extraction. [ACM-VIT/Weave-ml#149](https://github.com/ACM-VIT/Weave-ml/issues/149) remains authoritative for preprocessing, and [ACM-VIT/Weave-ml#28](https://github.com/ACM-VIT/Weave-ml/issues/28) for model qualification. Coordinate with the separate training-memory audit item if shared loader code changes.

- https://github.com/ACM-VIT/Weave-ml/blob/7da7fa8d6e947998ac634f64511c1af2f1f2ac03/Ranking_Training_module/train_ranker.py#L180

candidates.title: crash robot: one unreproduced projection_drift (facts fence empty, row present) under pooler_disconnect
candidates.taskDescription:
## What we saw
One local crash-robot replay on Postgres behind a transaction-mode PgBouncer failed with a `projection_drift` violation under the `pooler_disconnect` fault:

```
overlapping_slugs_two_sources seed=5105 pooler_disconnect: projection_drift:
  after ov6: robot-0/notes/alpha facts fence [] != rows ["Alpha fact mk-ov5"]
```

The run was on Bun 1.4.0 at about v0.60.463.0. The fact came from `ov5` (`remember`, committed). `ov6` was a `forget` refused `not_found`, so it wrote nothing. The check found the page's facts fence empty while the database still held the fact row as active.

## Reproduction attempts (none reproduced)
I replayed the failing manifest entry with `validate.ts --replay` on Postgres behind PgBouncer, at master e7bdf107b:
- 25 replays on Bun 1.4.0 and 25 on Bun 1.4.4, run sequentially: 0 failures.
- 24 replays with three robots running at once and two CPU spinners on a 4-vCPU machine (16 on Bun 1.4.0, 8 on Bun 1.4.4): 0 failures.
- 20 replays (10 per Bun version) with logging on the harness's page read: 0 failures, and no read errors were swallowed.

Before the failing run, about 30 earlier replays of the same entry also passed. That puts it at roughly 1 in 125 runs.

`pooler_disconnect` needs a Postgres admin connection, so this fault has no PGLite arm.

## Not the #7602 shape
#7602, fixed by #7606 in v0.60.462.0, is an `extract_facts` batch refused `revision_conflict` in facts-absorb, which then drops its facts. Here the fact came from `remember`, not extraction. The divergence also runs the other way: the fact row is present and only the page fence is missing it.

## Leading hypothesis: the harness read, not the store
`ReferenceModel.checkProjection` (`scripts/persistence/model.ts`) reads the page with `readPage` through `get_page`. `readPage` catches every error and returns `null`, and `checkProjection` then parses an empty string as the page content. `retryingRead` retries only errors that match `DROPPED_CONNECTION`. So a `get_page` that fails during a drop with any other error, such as a typed storage error, gives an empty fence while the rows are still there. That is exactly this signature, and the detail line shows nothing because `lastReadError` is not included in `projection_drift`.

This is unproven. It wasn't observed in 20 instrumented replays.

## Proposed next step
1. Have `checkProjection` treat a `null` read of a live page as a read failure. It should include `lastReadError` in the detail and not compare an empty string against the rows. The fence-equals-rows assertion stays.
2. If the drift recurs with a clean read, treat it as a real projection divergence. Use the retained fixture database to check whether the fence and rows converge after the drain.

The fixture manifest is kept in the crew drive as GBRA-135-pooler-projection-drift.json.
